This isn't algorithmic bias against under-served communities in the conventional sense, but it has equity implications I return to in the reflection. # Part 3 — feature engineering and improvements The error analysis points at three failure modes: 1. Rush-hour under-prediction at high-demand stations. 2. Calendar anomalies the existing features can't see 4 July, Labor Day, the late-August student return. 3. Spatial heterogeneity that station fixed effects absorb mechanically but don't explain. I add four features: ## Feature 1 — major holiday indicator ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} us_holidays_q3 <- as.Date(c("2024-07-04", "2024-09-02")) # July 4, Labor Day study_panel_complete <- study_panel_complete %>% mutate(holiday = ifelse(date %in% us_holidays_q3, 1, 0)) ``` ::: ## Feature 2 — university in session Penn and Temple fall classes started 26 August 2024; Drexel later (23 September). A binary flag from 26 August captures the bulk of the regime change. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fall_term_start <- as.Date("2024-08-26") study_panel_complete <- study_panel_complete %>% mutate(uni_in_session = ifelse(date >= fall_term_start, 1, 0)) ``` ::: ## Feature 3 — distance to City Hall A continuous spatial gradient capturing the demand falloff from Center City. Largely co-linear with station fixed effects but useful in models without them. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1635, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) stations_metric <- station_attributes %>% filter(!is.na(start_lat), !is.na(start_lon)) %>% st_as_sf(coords = c("start_lon", "start_lat"), crs = 4326) %>% st_transform(2272) # PA South State Plane (feet) city_hall_metric <- st_transform(city_hall, 2272) stations_metric <- stations_metric %>% mutate(dist_city_hall_km = as.numeric(st_distance(., city_hall_metric)) * 0.0003048) dist_lookup <- stations_metric %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(start_station, dist_city_hall_km) study_panel_complete <- study_panel_complete %>% left_join(dist_lookup, by = "start_station") ``` ::: ## Feature 4 — rolling 7-day station mean A station-level recent-demand level that updates through the quarter without leaking future information. Implemented as a 168-period lagged moving average via cumulative-sum differences. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} study_panel_complete <- study_panel_complete %>% arrange(start_station, interval60) %>% group_by(start_station) %>% mutate( cum_trips = cumsum(replace_na(Trip_Count, 0)), cum_trips_lag168 = lag(cum_trips, 168), cum_trips_lag1 = lag(cum_trips, 1), rolling_7day_mean = (cum_trips_lag1 - replace_na(cum_trips_lag168, 0)) / pmin(row_number() - 1, 168) ) %>% ungroup() %>% mutate(rolling_7day_mean = replace_na(rolling_7day_mean, 0)) %>% select(-cum_trips, -cum_trips_lag168, -cum_trips_lag1) ``` ::: ## Refit the train/test split with new features ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} train <- study_panel_complete %>% filter(week < cutoff_week) %>% mutate(dotw_simple = factor(dotw, levels = c("Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri","Sat","Sun"))) contrasts(train$dotw_simple) <- contr.treatment(7) test <- study_panel_complete %>% filter(week >= cutoff_week) %>% mutate(dotw_simple = factor(dotw, levels = c("Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri","Sat","Sun"))) contrasts(test$dotw_simple) <- contr.treatment(7) ``` ::: ## Model 6 — Model 5 plus all four new features ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model6 <- lm( Trip_Count ~ as.factor(hour) + dotw_simple + Temperature + Precipitation + lag1Hour + lag3Hours + lag1day + rush_hour + Med_Inc + Percent_Taking_Transit + Percent_White + as.factor(start_station) + rush_hour * weekend + holiday + uni_in_session + dist_city_hall_km + rolling_7day_mean, data = train ) cat("Model 6 R²:", summary(model6)$r.squared, " Adj R²:", summary(model6)$adj.r.squared, "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model 6 R²: 0.3469279 Adj R²: 0.3463542 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} summary(model6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = Trip_Count ~ as.factor(hour) + dotw_simple + Temperature + Precipitation + lag1Hour + lag3Hours + lag1day + rush_hour + Med_Inc + Percent_Taking_Transit + Percent_White + as.factor(start_station) + rush_hour * weekend + holiday + uni_in_session + dist_city_hall_km + rolling_7day_mean, data = train) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -5.9186 -0.5514 -0.1370 0.2945 21.5277 Coefficients: (7 not defined because of singularities) Estimate Std. This is a functional-form story, not a feature story: trip counts are counts, OLS is the wrong tool, and Poisson handles the mass at zero and the long tail correctly. # Brief report ## Quarter and rationale I chose Q3 2024 because summer is when Indego operates under most stress: highest ridership, tightest rebalancing constraints, and the largest cost of getting predictions wrong. The quarter also contains a real regime change, the late-August student return, which the in-class winter quarter could not see. ## Model comparison The five-step ladder behaves the way the in-class lab predicts. Model 1 (time and weather) gives MAE 0.825. Adding lags in Model 2 drops it to 0.711, a 14% improvement from one block of features, and almost the entire gain of the whole exercise before Poisson. Demographics, fixed effects, and the rush × weekend interaction add fractions of a hundredth of a trip each. Once the lags are in the model, the demographics and fixed effects are largely redundant with them: a station's recent demand pattern is what the demographic and FE variables were trying to proxy for, and the lags just measure it directly. The four new features in Model 6 reduce MAE by 0.001. The honest reading is that they didn't help. Switching to Poisson in Model 7 takes MAE from 0.707 to 0.662, bigger than every single feature addition after Model 2. Poisson is doing this by getting the functional form right, not by extracting new signal. ## Error analysis Three findings. First, errors track demand spatially. the worst-predicted stations are the busiest, in Center City and along the Schuylkill. This is partly mechanical (more trips means more variance to be wrong about) but it also tells us the model is missing structure that would help at high-volume stations specifically. Second, errors track demand temporally: PM rush on weekdays is the worst-fitting cell, which is exactly when rebalancing trucks have the least slack. Third, errors are higher in wealthier and whiter tracts because the busy stations are there. The model isn't biased against under-served neighbourhoods in the conventional sense; it formalises the existing demand gradient. ## New features and why Four features, motivated by the failure modes above. **Holiday flag** (4 July, Labor Day) for known calendar anomalies. **University in session** (≥ 26 August) for the late-August demand jump in University City and around Temple. **Distance to City Hall** for a continuous spatial gradient that station fixed effects absorb mechanically without explaining. **Rolling 7-day station mean** for a station-level recent-demand level that updates through the quarter. None of them moved overall MAE meaningfully. The most likely reason is that `lag1Hour` and `lag1day` already encode most of the station-specific demand information the new features were trying to add. The university flag is the most defensible on theoretical grounds, there's a real regime change at 26 August, but the lags adapt to the new pattern within a day or two, so the standalone flag earns little additional credit. ## Critical reflection on deployment Whether MAE 0.662 is good enough depends on the station and the decision. The mean trip count per station-hour in this test set sits below 1, most station-hours have 0 or 1 trips, so an MAE of 0.66 is comparable to typical demand at the median station. At a busy Center City station averaging 4 trips/hour, the same MAE is a 16% error, which is well within what truck-based rebalancing can absorb. At a quiet outer-Philadelphia station averaging 0.3 trips/hour, the same MAE is a 220% error and the model is worse than guessing the mean. The headline number hides this. I would deploy the model only for high-volume stations, with a fallback to a historical-average baseline at low-volume ones, and I would report predictions as ranges rather than as single numbers. Errors are higher in Center City than in West, North, or South Philadelphia, but average demand is higher there too. If Indego rebalances proactively in proportion to predicted demand, the wealthier high-demand stations get more truck-time, which is what already happens. The safeguard worth flagging is monitoring relative error (MAE / average demand) by tract demographics rather than absolute error, so that systematically poor predictions in low-demand neighbourhoods aren't masked by their small absolute size. The model is blind to two things that obviously matter. Events; Phillies games, concerts at the Mann, conventions are absent and would explain a chunk of the residual variance, especially the high-demand-tail under-prediction. Station supply constraints are also absent: a station with no bikes can't generate trips even when demand is high, and a station with no docks can't receive a return. Beyond these, the linear and Poisson specifications both assume a fairly stable functional relationship, and the 4 July spike shows that real ridership has fat tails neither handles well.
